new.statement: Sample efficiency dominates time-to-75%: an airbench-style whitened CNN (frozen patch-whitening, dirac init, BN, Nesterov SGD, label smoothing, Lookahead) needs far fewer epochs to reach 75% on CIFAR-100 than ResNet-style baselines. The best time is mostly set by epochs x FLOPs/epoch on that architecture family.

An airbench96-family net (128/384/512, last block widened to 576, 3 convs per block) trained with the airbench96 SGD settings sits near the 75% edge at about 8.5 epochs without TTA. Its accuracy vs epochs curve is smooth, so the cheapest feasible epoch count can be found by interpolation.

Reproduction: airbench96 128/384/576, 8.5 epochs, batch 1024, no TTA, compile+warmup in build gives a 3-seed accuracy >= 0.753 and time <= 9.0 s on this A100-SXM4. Repeating the identical run twice gives a 3-seed-mean accuracy spread <= 0.3 pp and a time spread <= 0.2 s, which sets the noise floor for later verdicts.

Epoch sweep on the H1a1 recipe at 7, 8.5 and 10 epochs: accuracy rises monotonically by 0.4-1.0 pp per epoch and crosses 0.753 between 8 and 9.5 epochs. Time scales close to linearly with epochs, with an intercept <= 1.0 s.

Width/depth trade-off: a narrower airbench-style net trained for more epochs reaches 75% in less wall time than the 128/384/576 net at 8.5 epochs, because FLOPs/epoch falls faster than epochs-to-75% rises.
A 96/256/384 (or 128/256/384) airbench96-layout net, at whatever epoch count gives 3-seed accuracy >= 0.753, finishes at least 10% faster than the best feasible 128/384/576 configuration.
Frozen patch-whitening and dirac init are the main sample-efficiency components on CIFAR-100, as they are on CIFAR-10. Removing them raises epochs-to-75% substantially.
At a fixed epoch count near the feasibility edge, replacing frozen whitening init with a standard learned first conv lowers 3-seed accuracy by >= 1.0 pp, which is well outside noise.

Per-epoch throughput and fixed overhead are a large share of the score at the ~8 s scale. GPU-resident data and augmentation, fp16/bf16 channels_last, compile max-autotune and CUDA graphs captured in build, larger batches, and a cheap prepare (transfer and whitening PCA) cut time without changing accuracy.

With only 4 pinned CPU cores, any CPU-side data pipeline (DataLoader, CPU augmentation) bottlenecks training. Holding the whole uint8 dataset on the GPU and doing flip, translate and cutout on the GPU removes that bottleneck.

Baseline: the unmodified submission_template recipe runs feasibly at roughly 50-70 s. Swapping only its data pipeline for a GPU-resident one with GPU augmentation cuts time by >= 20% with accuracy within +/-0.3 pp.

At batch ~1024 and ~400 steps per run, kernel-launch and Python overhead is significant. torch.compile(mode='max-autotune') or CUDA-graph capture in the untimed build reduces s/step. Eval must use a separate dynamic or padded path that stays legal for any B in 1..1024.

On the feasible airbench96 recipe, switching from default compile to max-autotune plus CUDA-graph capture of the train step cuts mean time by >= 8% with |delta accuracy| < 0.3 pp. Eval for B in {1, 7, 1024} completes in < 5 s.

Timed prepare work (GPU transfer, normalization, whitening PCA over all patches) is a non-negligible fixed cost. Computing whitening on a patch subset and fusing preprocessing shrinks it at no accuracy cost.
Computing the whitening eigendecomposition on <= 5,000 images instead of the full set cuts mean time by >= 0.15 s, with accuracy change within noise (|delta| < 0.3 pp).

Doing less compute per epoch beats running fewer epochs: hard-example filtering and progressive resizing cut FLOPs per useful gradient enough to lower time-to-75% on CIFAR-100, even in a short, under-fitting schedule.

Proxy-based data filtering: a tiny proxy net scores each batch, and the main net trains only on the highest-loss half. This saves more backward compute than the proxy pass and the extra epochs cost, as airbench96_faster does on CIFAR-10.

airbench96_faster-style filtering (proxy 32/64/64, keep the top 50% by loss) on the best feasible recipe reaches 3-seed accuracy >= 0.753 at a mean time at least 10% lower than the best unfiltered feasible run.
Progressive resizing: training the early epochs at reduced resolution (e.g. 24 px) costs little final accuracy, because early epochs learn coarse features, and it cuts their FLOPs by about 44%.

Training the first ~50% of epochs at 24 px and the rest at 32 px cuts time by >= 10% compared with a 32 px run of equal epoch count, with accuracy loss <= 0.3 pp. Compiled graphs for both resolutions are built in build.

The airbench96 CIFAR-10 hyperparameters are mis-tuned for a short (~8 epoch) 100-class run. Re-tuning regularization and the schedule for the under-fitting regime raises accuracy at fixed epochs, which lets the epoch count be cut. Hyperparameter-only gains are expected to be modest (<~10% time).

At ~8 epochs the model under-fits, so the airbench96 augmentation (cutout 12, translate 4) and label smoothing 0.2 over-regularize. Weaker augmentation and less smoothing improve accuracy at fixed epochs.
At a fixed epoch count near the edge, removing cutout (or cutting it to 8 px) and lowering label smoothing to 0.1 raises 3-seed accuracy by >= 0.4 pp over the airbench96 defaults.

Optimizer choice: Muon on conv filters, which set the CIFAR-10 record, does not beat tuned Nesterov SGD on the airbench96 net for CIFAR-100. Prior evidence leans toward refutation, so this is low-priority and needs only one decisive check.

new.statement: Replacing SGD with Muon (lr ~0.24, momentum 0.6) on the conv filters of the feasible airbench96 recipe at equal epochs raises 3-seed accuracy by >= 0.3 pp. Expected outcome: refuted.
Alternating (derandomized) horizontal flip gives a better gradient signal than random flip at short budgets, so it improves accuracy at fixed epochs on CIFAR-100 as it does on CIFAR-10.
Switching from random flip to alternating flip at a fixed epoch count near the edge raises 3-seed accuracy by >= 0.3 pp at the same time cost.

structured_output.summary:
The tree was empty, so I seeded it with 4 top-level (Lvl1) hypotheses, each with mechanisms (Lvl2) and falsifiable predictions (Lvl3):

- **H1, sample efficiency:** an airbench96-family whitened CNN at about 8.5 epochs is the main lever. The anchor prediction is that the public 8.11 s / 75.29% result reproduces here. It also covers an epoch sweep, a width-vs-epochs trade-off, and an ablation of whitening and dirac init.
- **H2, throughput and overhead:** keeping data and augmentation on the GPU (only 4 CPU cores are available), compile max-autotune and CUDA graphs prepared in the untimed build, and a cheaper whitening step in prepare.
- **H3, less compute per epoch:** airbench96_faster-style hard-example filtering, and training early epochs at lower resolution.
- **H4, hyperparameters for a short 100-class run:** weaker cutout and label smoothing, alternating flip, and Muon. Prior evidence says Muon lost to SGD, so it starts at low confidence and is expected to be refuted.

No updates, because there is no evidence yet. Following the review, the first runs should be:
- the unmodified template as a baseline (H2a1);
- the airbench96 reproduction, run twice to measure accuracy and time noise (H1a1).

Until that noise floor is measured, any accuracy change under about 0.3 pp, or any time change within the measured jitter, should be logged as inconclusive. Every candidate also needs a rule check:
- no real data in build;
- a full reset in prepare;
- eval that works for any batch size from 1 to 1024 within 5 s;
- no TTA.

Absolute times measured on this SXM GPU won't carry over to the PCIe judging GPU.
